subproblem.title: Markov selection of a good parameter in an interval
subproblem.statement: Let g : ℝ → [0, ∞] be almost-everywhere measurable for Lebesgue measure, p a predicate on ℝ that holds for Lebesgue-almost every t, a < b real numbers and I ∈ [0, ∞] with ∫_{(a,b)} g dL¹ ≤ I (lower Lebesgue integral over Ioo a b). Then there is t ∈ (a, b) with p(t) and (b − a)·g(t) ≤ 2·I, computed in [0, ∞] with b − a embedded by ENNReal.ofReal.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (g : ℝ → ℝ≥0∞) (p : ℝ → Prop) (a b : ℝ) (I : ℝ≥0∞), a < b → AEMeasurable g → (∀ᵐ t, p t) → ∫⁻ t in Ioo a b, g t ≤ I → ∃ t ∈ Ioo a b, p t ∧ ENNReal.ofReal (b - a) * g t ≤ 2 * I
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof (Markov's inequality on the interval (ρ_ν/2, ρ_ν) to pick a radius in the a.e. set of (SL2)). Notation: c := ENNReal.ofReal(b − a); since a < b we have 0 < c < ∞ and volume(Ioo a b) = c (Real.volume_Ioo). Write ν := volume.restrict (Ioo a b).
1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that the conclusion fails: for every t ∈ Ioo a b with p(t) we have 2·I < c·g(t) (push_neg).
2. Since p holds volume-a.e., for ν-a.e. t we have 2·I < c·g(t): by ae_restrict_iff' measurableSet_Ioo it suffices that for volume-a.e. t, t ∈ Ioo a b → 2·I < c·g(t), which follows from the a.e. statement for p and step 1 (filter_upwards).
3. A null-interval contradiction. If ∀ᵐ t ∂ν, False, then ν univ = 0 (ae_iff), i.e. volume(Ioo a b) = 0 (Measure.restrict_apply_univ), contradicting volume(Ioo a b) = c > 0.
4. Case I = ∞. Then 2·I = ∞ and ∞ < c·g(t) is impossible, so step 2 gives ∀ᵐ t ∂ν, False; contradiction by step 3.
5. Case I < ∞. By lintegral_mono_ae applied to the a.e. inequality 2·I ≤ c·g(t) of step 2: ∫⁻ t, 2·I ∂ν ≤ ∫⁻ t, c·g(t) ∂ν. The left side is 2·I·volume(Ioo a b) = 2·I·c (setLIntegral_const). The right side is c·∫⁻_{Ioo a b} g (lintegral_const_mul'' with the a.e.-measurability of g for ν, AEMeasurable.restrict), which is ≤ c·I by hypothesis. Hence 2·I·c ≤ c·I. As c ≠ 0 and c ≠ ∞ we may cancel c (ENNReal.mul_le_mul_right) and get 2·I ≤ I; since I < ∞ this forces I = 0 (for instance pass to toReal: 2x ≤ x with x ≥ 0 gives x = 0).
6. Then ∫⁻_{Ioo a b} g ≤ 0, so g = 0 ν-a.e. (lintegral_eq_zero_iff' with the a.e.-measurability of g for ν). With I = 0, step 2 says 0 < c·g(t) for ν-a.e. t; combining, for ν-a.e. t we get 0 < c·0 = 0, i.e. ∀ᵐ t ∂ν, False, contradicting step 3.
7. Both cases are contradictory, so some t ∈ Ioo a b satisfies p(t) and ENNReal.ofReal(b − a)·g(t) ≤ 2·I. ∎
proof_key_steps: Assume every t ∈ (a,b) with p(t) has 2I < (b−a)g(t); then this holds a.e. on (a,b).
If I = ∞ the a.e. inequality is impossible, so (a,b) would be null.
If I < ∞, integrating gives 2I(b−a) ≤ (b−a)∫g ≤ (b−a)I, hence I = 0.
With I = 0, g = 0 a.e. on (a,b) contradicts 0 < (b−a)g a.e.; so a good t exists.

audit.reason: The contradiction argument correctly handles I = infinity, finite positive I, and I = 0. Restriction of the a.e. hypotheses, cancellation of the finite positive interval length, and the zero-integral argument establish the exact conclusion.
